content: 1. Children diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB) should be registered with the National Tuberculosis Program (NTP). This requirement applies to all healthcare services and programs, including public non-NTP services, private-sector facilities, and practitioners where children and adolescents with TB are diagnosed. 2. Underreporting of TB cases in children and adolescents in these sectors contributes significantly to the high proportion of undiagnosed or missing cases of TB in this population. 3. Children and adolescents diagnosed with TB in hospitals who die before treatment initiation or discharge must also be registered with the NTP. 4. Local monitoring of specimen collection, diagnostic tests, results, and clinical diagnoses in a TB laboratory register (or equivalent system) is recommended to ensure accurate tracking and reporting. 5. In countries with case-based electronic recording and reporting systems, all children and adolescents treated for TB should be reported to the NTP in one of four age bands: 0–4 years, 5–9 years, 10–14 years, and 15–19 years. 6. The diagnostic category, treatment regimen, and treatment start date should be recorded on the child’s growth monitoring card, TB treatment card, and the health unit TB register. 7. The child’s weight should be recorded at each visit on their growth monitoring card and TB treatment card, as weight is critical for monitoring treatment response and adjusting medication dosages. 8. Treatment outcomes for all children and adolescents should be recorded in the TB register and reported to the NTP. Outcome categories for children and adolescents are the same as those for adults. 9. Few younger children with TB meet the criteria for being classified as cured because they are less likely to have bacteriologically confirmed TB. 10. In most settings, children who cannot expectorate sputum are not routinely retested for bacteriological response beyond the two-month assessment unless there are indications of poor treatment response. 11. The principles of TB treatment in children and adolescents are the same as those for adults. However, specific regimens are recommended based on age and disease severity: For children aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe drug-susceptible TB, a 4-month regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR) is recommended. For adolescents aged 12 years and older, a 4-month treatment regimen (2HPMZ/2HMP) may be used, regardless of pulmonary TB disease severity. For children with TB meningitis (TBM), a 6-month intensive treatment regimen (6HRZEto) may be used as an alternative to the standard 12-month regimen (2HRZE/10HR). 12. Child-friendly dispersible fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets should be used for children weighing less than 25 kg. 13. Children typically gain weight during TB treatment, and dosages should be adjusted accordingly. 14. A caregiver should be identified as a treatment supporter for children of all ages, including older children and adolescents. 15. Adherence to the full course of treatment should be emphasized and reinforced to ensure successful outcomes. 16. TB medicines are generally well-tolerated in children and adolescents, with side effects being uncommon. The most important adverse event to monitor is hepatotoxicity. 17. Ethambutol can be safely used in children at recommended dosages. 18. For children and adolescents with multidrug-resistant (MDR) or rifampicin-resistant (RR) TB, treatment should follow WHO-recommended regimens. These regimens prioritize the use of all-oral, bedaquiline-containing shorter regimens when possible. 19. Bedaquiline and delamanid are now recommended for use in children of all ages as part of MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens. These drugs allow for the construction of all-oral treatment regimens. 20. For longer individualized regimens, at least four effective TB agents should be included at the start of treatment, with at least three agents maintained throughout the course if bedaquiline is stopped. 21. Injectable agents (e.g., aminoglycosides) are associated with hearing loss and should be avoided in young children due to the difficulty of monitoring and the potential impact on cognitive and language development. 22. The inclusion of specific drugs in MDR/RR-TB regimens should be guided by drug susceptibility testing (DST) results and the history of exposure to TB medicines. 23. Contact investigation and screening of child and adolescent contacts of infectious MDR/RR-TB cases are essential for early diagnosis and prompt treatment initiation. 24. Improving case-finding, particularly among young children with MDR/RR-TB, is critical to reducing the risk of poor outcomes. 25. WHO guidelines recommend prioritizing standardized shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimens for eligible patients with MDR/RR-TB. For those not eligible, individualized longer regimens should be constructed using drugs from priority groupings (A, B, and C). 26. The risks and benefits of each medicine should be carefully considered when designing a treatment regimen. Most TB medicines are well-tolerated, but some, such as injectable agents, carry significant risks. 27. Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, linezolid, clofazimine, and cycloserine/terizidone are recommended for inclusion in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens, depending on the patient’s specific needs and drug susceptibility. 28. Ethionamide, prothionamide, and para-aminosalicylic acid should only be used in longer regimens if better options are unavailable, as their use is generally discouraged due to limited efficacy and higher toxicity. 29. Clavulanic acid should not be included in MDR/RR-TB regimens, except as part of formulations combined with amoxicillin for specific indications.
